title: Phonographs, waltzes and quadrilles before radio
summary: She describes long-horn phonographs, waltzing, two-steps, polka and quadrille before radio.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: The pieces, the popular pieces sounded just as fine as the old ones, but they always played with a powerful beat and a variation, you know. Have you ever noticed when, like they're playing on, you're hearing orchestra on television, how they put all that variation on the piano and all. That's not in the piece, but just do that. Have you noticed on Lawrence Waltz, the piano, that girl that plays? She just can put it on. But I don't believe you'd call that ragtime, would you? The way she goes at it. Yeah, you notice her on a Saturday, Lawrence Waltz, that girl that plays the piano. But he has some lovely waltzing on his program. Well, this was before radio time at that time. And that's the time we used to have the phonograph with good records, with the long horn phonographs in those days, you see. We didn't have the phonographs without the horn. They had this long horn. You danced waltzes then? We went to dance waltzes and two steps. Quad wheels and polka. Quad wheel? You never heard of that?
I don't know, it was some kind of different step. Your mother would know if you'd ask, I bet you. She heard of it.
It's kind of like a square dance in a way, they have a call for that.
